result:
I’ve been thinking lately about how people are starting to treat time as if it were a fold-out map rather than a single, one-way street. A map invites detours: you can trace the roads you’ve already followed, imagine shortcuts that never existed, or wonder what might lie beyond the edge where the printer ran out of ink. Time, meanwhile, still only flows forward—yet our technologies, stories, and collective habits keep trying to flatten it into something we can refold at will.

Consider smartphones’ photo galleries. Each swipe is a wormhole: a baked-in, low-stakes form of time travel. You thumb back through thumbnails of birthday cakes, plane wings framed by orange sunsets, blurry concert lights, and the accidental close-ups of your own shoes. Moments that were once irrevocably “spent” now feel almost retrievable, a kind of rented nostalgia. But the rent comes due in subtle ways. A notification pops up—“On this day, five years ago…”—and suddenly you’re cross-examining a past version of yourself, checking whether the present has measured up. Memory becomes less a cathedral of treasured relics and more a searchable, monetized database. 

Fiction writers have intuited this tension for ages. In Jorge Luis Borges’s “The Garden of Forking Paths,” every possible future splits off into its own branch. In Octavia Butler’s “Kindred,” modern memory collides with historical trauma as a contemporary woman is yanked backward into slavery-era Maryland. What both stories suggest is that time’s apparent linearity is fragile; personal and cultural memories can tug at it, crease it, sometimes tear it.  

And then there’s the accelerating role of artificial intelligence. Large language models like me ingest enormous swaths of the past—books, websites, forum posts—then recombine their patterns to generate something that feels new. When you ask for a poem or a business plan, you’re really asking a trillion-parameter crystal ball to echo the aggregated memory of humanity, minus its timestamps. In a sense the model has no present tense at all; it’s an eternal remix of yesterday. That evokes a paradox: people build AI to navigate the future more effectively, yet the machine’s entire mental scaffolding is a fossil record.

Architecture offers a counter-argument: buildings that literally breathe time. There’s a trend toward “adaptive reuse,” in which abandoned factories become art studios or shopping hubs; century-old churches turn into co-working lofts; coal plants morph into solar farms. These spaces refuse to pretend the past never happened. You’ll see new steel beams hugging old brick, glass catwalks suspended above riveted iron columns. Walking through such places, you feel multiple eras talking to one another. The effect is optimistic: if a derelict smokestack can house dove-white servers and hydroponic basil, maybe individuals, too, can host more than one life within a single lifetime.

So what practical lesson unfolds from all this? Perhaps it’s that we should treat memory as compost rather than crystal. Bury the shards of yesterday in the soil of attention, let them decay, let them feed whatever is next. The past becomes nutrient, not burden. That mindset disciplines how we archive our digital footprints: do we need every screenshot forever? Do we want algorithms to decide which memories gain prime real estate in our lives? Instead of hoarding, we might curate—and instead of curating solely for nostalgia, we might compost for possibility.  

The cartographers of old used to ink dragons onto the corners of the map where knowledge ended. In our age, the dragons do not mark what’s unreachable; they mark what’s unanalyzed, untagged, untreated as data. And maybe that’s healthy. Some events deserve to evaporate into rumor, poetry, uncertainty. The unknown keeps the future weird enough to matter.

So I vote we keep making things—stories, software, buildings—that remember just enough to enrich the present but forget enough to give tomorrow room to surprise us. If time can’t actually fold, the least we can do is refuse to live on a single, predictable line. Let the map stay creased, dog-eared, coffee-stained, and half-drawn. That is where wonder sneaks in and takes up residence.
